answer:
Based on my research, I can now answer this question.

**Undercovers** aired on **NBC** (its original network). The three major U.S. broadcast networks based in New York are **NBC**, **CBS**, and **ABC**.

Among these three, **CBS** (Columbia Broadcasting System) bought the UK record label **Oriole Records** in 1964. According to the sources:

- CBS launched its own CBS Records label in the UK in 1962, but EMI owned rights to the Columbia name there
- In September 1964, CBS acquired Oriole Records, which gave CBS Records its own distribution and pressing facilities in the UK
- The Colnbrook plant from Oriole was acquired and CBS began distributing through its newly-owned Oriental facilities starting in 1965

**The answer is: Oriole Records**

"Undercovers" is an American action thriller television series directed by J.J. Abrams, who also co-wrote the series with Josh Reims. Starring Boris Kodjoe, Gugu Mbatha-Raw, Jessica Parker Kennedy, Gerald McRaney, and Carter MacIntyre, the series premiered on NBC on September 22, 2010, and consists of 13 episodes.
14
Produced by Abrams' team, known for "Lost", the series was likened to a television version of "Mr. & Mrs. Smith". The plot revolves around former CIA agent couple Steven Bloom and Samantha Bloom. After five years in retirement, they are pulled back into service by intelligence officer Carlton Shaw to investigate the disappearance of their former colleague, Leo Nash. As they undertake missions in locations such as Berlin and Madrid to unravel confidential crises, they face dual challenges of their spy identities and their marital relationship.
12
Although the production team denied any connection to "Alias", the plot structure sparked discussions about similarities. Due to consistently low ratings, NBC canceled the series mid-season, leaving the remaining episodes unaired in their entirety.
13

Cast Introduction
Boris Kodjoe
Boris Kodjoe portrayed Steven Bloom in the NBC spy series "Undercovers". He is the husband of Samantha Bloom (played by Gugu Mbatha-Raw) and is one of the CIA's most renowned spies.
3
Kodjoe was born in Vienna, Austria, and grew up in Germany. He was once named one of the "World's 50 Most Beautiful People" by People magazine and has appeared in a series of films and television shows.
Perhaps Kodjoe is best known from the Showtime drama "Soul Food", a role which led to his marriage to his co-star Nicole Ari Parker and also earned him three NAACP Image Award nominations. He later starred alongside Parker in the sitcom "The Undoing", for which he also served as a producer.
His film credits include Spike Lee's "Love & Basketball", "Brown Sugar", "The Gospel", "Madea's Family Reunion", "The World Unseen", and "Starship Troopers 3: Marauder". In "Brown Sugar", he starred alongside Taye Diggs and Queen Latifah. He played opposite Bruce Willis in the action thriller "Surrogates" and also appeared in the thriller "Resident Evil: Afterlife", directed by Paul W.S. Anderson and released in September.
Undercovers Highlight Moments
In 2009, he made his Broadway debut in Tennessee Williams' classic play "Cat on a Hot Tin Roof", which featured a cast including James Earl Jones, Phylicia Rashad, Anika Noni Rose, and Giancarlo Esposito.
Prior to embarking on his acting career, he worked as a model for Ford Models, where he modeled for brands such as Ralph Lauren, Perry Ellis, Yves Saint Laurent, and The Gap. Leveraging his background in the fashion industry, he co-founded his own clothing company, ALFA, with his partner, Patrick.
Kodjoe's primary personal interest lies in fundraising for Sophie's Voice Foundation, a foundation he and his wife host in honor of their daughter Sophie, who was diagnosed with spina bifida at birth.
He and Nicole have two children and currently reside in Los Angeles.
Gugu Mbatha-Raw

Gugu Mbatha-Raw portrays Samantha Bloom, the wife of Steven Bloom (played by Boris Kodjoe) and one of the CIA's top agents in the NBC spy series Undercovers.
4
Born in Oxford, England, Mbatha-Raw is a bona fide graduate of the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art. Well-versed in Shakespeare, her first professional performance was in an open-air production of As You Like It, playing Celia. She subsequently performed in Antony and Cleopatra at the Royal Exchange Theatre in Manchester and as the lead, Juliet, in Romeo and Juliet, earning her a nomination for the Manchester Evening News Best Actress Award in 2005.
Her British television credits include Spooks, Doctor Who, Marple: A Murder Is Announced, Bonekickers, and Foyle's War. It was her role in the latter that led to her being selected by Screen International magazine as a Star of Tomorrow in 2008.
Her other stage work includes performances in "Big White Fog" at the Almeida Theatre and "Gethsemane" at the National Theatre, which subsequently toured the UK. Mbatha-Raw made her West End debut playing Ophelia opposite Jude Law in a production of "Hamlet." The production transferred to the United States and became a major success, turning into a hit Broadway show in 2009.
Mbatha-Raw's first film, "Larry Crowne," began shooting in Los Angeles. Directed by Tom Hanks, she starred alongside Julia Roberts, traveling between London and Los Angeles for the production.
Gerald McRaney
CARLTON SHAW
5
Gerald McRaney played Carlton Shaw, a CIA liaison and the handler who gives orders to Steven and Samantha, in the NBC spy drama series "Undercovers." To date, Gerald McRaney has worked on television for over 16 years and has delivered notable performances in numerous series such as "Simon & Simon," "Major Dad," "The Promised Land," "Deadwood," "Jericho," and "JAG." His career has reached new heights, and he is thoroughly enjoying it.
6

In the previous season, he also made his Broadway debut in Horton Foote's play "Dividing the Estate." He later appeared in the independent film "Get Low," alongside Oscar-nominated actor Robert Duvall, Golden Globe-nominated actor Bill Murray, Oscar winner Sissy Spacek, and Lucas Black. He also co-starred with Liam Neeson and Bradley Cooper in the action-adventure film "The A-Team."
His first television role was a guest appearance on "Night Gallery," followed by several appearances on "Gunsmoke." He then began to appear in numerous television movies, such as "Where the Ladies Go," "The White Shadow," "The Law," and "Roots: The Next Generations." He also appeared in classic series like "The Incredible Hulk," "The Rockford Files," and "How the West Was Won."
In addition, McRaney has appeared in many highly-rated television series. These include the television movies "The John Denver Story," "A Stranger Beside Me," "Not My Son," "The Death of a Centerfold: The Dorothy Stratten Story," "Dream of Murder," and "Someone She Knows." The talented McRaney also crossed over into directing multiple film and television projects, such as "The Two Simons" and "Major Dad," while also serving as a producer on several works. He has collaborated with his wife, actress Delta Burke.
Carter MacIntyre
LEO NASH
7
Carter MacIntyre portrayed LEO NASH in the NBC spy drama series "Undercovers," an elusive agent working under Steven and Samantha (played by Boris Kodjoe and Gugu Mbatha-Raw). MacIntyre previously played the rogue hero JD Bruce in the series "American Heiress." He has also guest-starred in numerous series including "Nip/Tuck," "It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia," "The Mentalist," "Trauma," and "Bones."
8
He has also appeared in several films, including "The Choice of Fate," starring Louis Gossett Jr. and Lauren Holly, and "The Truth," starring John Heard.
MacIntyre is from Atlanta, Georgia, and graduated from Wake Forest University in North Carolina. He enjoys playing tennis and golf, reading, and traveling. He is single and currently resides in Los Angeles.
Highlights

The first regular series officially picked up for the 2010-2011 season by the five major networks has finally been announced -- Undercovers. This likely comes as no surprise, as the spy comedy created by J.J. Abrams and Josh Reims (Brothers & Sisters) has been one of NBC's hottest new series for 2013. NBC's President of Primetime Entertainment, Angela Bromstad, lavished praise on J.J. Abrams when announcing the pickup, stating that J.J.'s involvement was "something worth celebrating in a big way."
Synopsis
Overview
Stills
9
Undercovers was created by the renowned writer, producer, and director J.J. Abrams, known for series such as Lost, Alias, and Fringe, along with producer and writer Josh Reims from Brothers & Sisters and What About Brian. It is a spy drama filled with sexiness, humor, and action, exploring the idea that in the world of espionage, working as a married couple has its pros and cons, but danger is a constant. On the surface, Steven Bloom (played by Boris Kodjoe
) and his wife Samantha (played by Gugu Mbatha-Raw) are a happy couple. They own a small catering company in Los Angeles and lead a typical middle-class life. Samantha's sister, Lizzy (played by
Jessica Parker Kennedy
), also helps out at the company, but she is not particularly ambitious.
In reality, Steven and Samantha are top agents trained by the
Central Intelligence Agency
(CIA). They fell in love five years ago while on a mission and subsequently decided to retire. When their friend and colleague Leo Nash (played by
Carter MacIntyre
) mysteriously disappears while tracking a Russian arms magnate, CIA official Carlton Shaw (played by Gerald McRaney) is forced to ask the Bloom couple to come out of retirement. The concern is that Nash possesses sensitive intelligence, and its potential leak could have dire consequences. They are tasked with finding and rescuing Nash.
The Blooms are initially reluctant to get involved but ultimately cannot refuse. Furthermore, they quickly discover that being "undercover spies" is more tense, thrilling, exciting, and romantic than being "full-time spies"—elements that had been missing from their marriage for a long time.
First Episode Synopsis

Steven Bloom and Samantha Bloom have been out of the CIA for five years. They are married, have started a family, and together with Samantha's sister Lizzy, they run a small catering business, living a normal life. Their marriage is stable and happy, and everything seems perfect. An international hotel chain is preparing to host a series of events and hires the Blooms as catering consultants. The Blooms never imagined that their peaceful life was about to end...
10
The Blooms' former CIA supervisor, Agent Garlton Shaw, locates them through the hotel and asks them to return to work for the Agency. The Blooms flatly refuse: "We don't want to lose the life we have now. We've worked hard for five years in Los Angeles to build what we have." However, Shaw's visit stirs up old memories for the Blooms... Days later, they embark on a new mission. Samantha's former field partner, Leo Nash, has mysteriously disappeared while tracking Russian arms dealer Alexander Schlotsky, and the CIA suspects Leo may have turned. Leo is one of the CIA's top operatives, known for his elusive nature. The Blooms have a close history with him; perhaps only they know where to find him—which is the main reason the CIA has recalled them.
The Blooms quickly discover that Leo was last seen in
Madrid
, Spain, and rush there to investigate with the help of the local CIA action officer, Bill Hoyt (played by Ben Schwartz). Bill makes no secret of his admiration for Steven, and his flattery makes Samantha uncomfortable. Steven, for his part, is also uneasy about Samantha and Leo's "complicated past."
They sneak into a bank to review security footage, pose as wedding guests to find Leo's contact... After this series of by-the-book "spycraft," they finally uncover the mystery behind Leo's disappearance. The Blooms' blood starts pumping... It's been a long time since they felt this kind of excitement. Perhaps it's only in "the game" that they can rediscover their old passion.
The mission may be over, but the Blooms' life as spies is far from finished. It's just that... now they are catering contractors by day and operatives by night.
Synopsis of Episode 3
Episode 3 Stills
11

In Episode 3 of Undercovers, an individual claims to possess crucial information regarding a code-breaking device that could potentially expose the true identities of every CIA agent. Shaw orders Steven and Samantha Bloom to travel to Berlin to verify the intelligence. They quickly discover that the informant has been killed. With the assistance of Bill Hoyt and Leo Nash, they uncover the truth behind the entire incident. Meanwhile, Steven and Samantha continue to struggle with the awkward dynamic of being both partners and spouses while on missions.
12
Brief Review
Despite the production team's repeated denials of any resemblance to Alias, the two shows do share factual similarities (such as the chase sequence in the opening minutes). This is not necessarily a bad thing—spy shows often rely on familiar tropes, and if a series cannot achieve the "revolutionary innovation" of a show like Chuck, it might be better to stick to convention.
13
Some expressed concern that the show, featuring an all-Black lead cast (a first in recent years), might not be accepted by audiences. This worry seems somewhat justified, but not entirely—both lead actors are "quite attractive" Black individuals, though they have limited acting experience and are less familiar to viewers. "Spotlighting newcomers" has been J.J. Abrams' consistent approach, and the "newcomers" he selects are generally reliable (e.g., Keri Russell, Evangeline Lilly, Jennifer Garner, Anna Torv).
This series feels more like a marital relationship drama or a light comedy than a traditional spy thriller. It is the most relaxed, straightforward, and least intellectually demanding of all J.J. Abrams' works—even simpler than the relationship drama Felicity. Furthermore, Steven and Samantha's adversaries are all paper tigers, even more inept than the enemies faced by Christopher Chance in Human Target. At least in the premiere episode, the Blooms never encounter any real danger.
Some have bluntly pointed out that if this series were not associated with J.J. Abrams in any way, it would not have garnered its current level of attention.
Series Cancellation

After another painful decline in ratings, NBC officially announced the cancellation of J.J. Abrams' series Undercovers (5.8 million viewers, 1.3 rating in the 18-49 demographic). NBC will air the three remaining completed episodes (episodes 8-10) as scheduled. As for whether episodes 11-13 might ever air, that's anyone's guess. This is the second series bearing J.J. Abrams' name to be canceled mid-season, the previous one being Six Degrees. Undercovers had also received a four-episode back-order. Similarly, Undercovers' ratings were struggling on the edge, but the show's creativity was certainly commendable and deserved more attention.

Cast Introduction
Boris Kodjoe
Boris Kodjoe portrayed Steven Bloom in the NBC spy series "Undercovers". He is the husband of Samantha Bloom (played by Gugu Mbatha-Raw) and is one of the CIA's most renowned spies.
3
Kodjoe was born in Vienna, Austria, and grew up in Germany. He was once named one of the "World's 50 Most Beautiful People" by People magazine and has appeared in a series of films and television shows.
Perhaps Kodjoe is best known from the Showtime drama "Soul Food", a role which led to his marriage to his co-star Nicole Ari Parker and also earned him three NAACP Image Award nominations. He later starred alongside Parker in the sitcom "The Undoing", for which he also served as a producer.
His film credits include Spike Lee's "Love & Basketball", "Brown Sugar", "The Gospel", "Madea's Family Reunion", "The World Unseen", and "Starship Troopers 3: Marauder". In "Brown Sugar", he starred alongside Taye Diggs and Queen Latifah. He played opposite Bruce Willis in the action thriller "Surrogates" and also appeared in the thriller "Resident Evil: Afterlife", directed by Paul W.S. Anderson and released in September.
Undercovers Highlight Moments
In 2009, he made his Broadway debut in Tennessee Williams' classic play "Cat on a Hot Tin Roof", which featured a cast including James Earl Jones, Phylicia Rashad, Anika Noni Rose, and Giancarlo Esposito.
Prior to embarking on his acting career, he worked as a model for Ford Models, where he modeled for brands such as Ralph Lauren, Perry Ellis, Yves Saint Laurent, and The Gap. Leveraging his background in the fashion industry, he co-founded his own clothing company, ALFA, with his partner, Patrick.
Kodjoe's primary personal interest lies in fundraising for Sophie's Voice Foundation, a foundation he and his wife host in honor of their daughter Sophie, who was diagnosed with spina bifida at birth.
He and Nicole have two children and currently reside in Los Angeles.
Gugu Mbatha-Raw
texts.2:
Gugu Mbatha-Raw portrays Samantha Bloom, the wife of Steven Bloom (played by Boris Kodjoe) and one of the CIA's top agents in the NBC spy series Undercovers.
4
Born in Oxford, England, Mbatha-Raw is a bona fide graduate of the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art. Well-versed in Shakespeare, her first professional performance was in an open-air production of As You Like It, playing Celia. She subsequently performed in Antony and Cleopatra at the Royal Exchange Theatre in Manchester and as the lead, Juliet, in Romeo and Juliet, earning her a nomination for the Manchester Evening News Best Actress Award in 2005.
Her British television credits include Spooks, Doctor Who, Marple: A Murder Is Announced, Bonekickers, and Foyle's War. It was her role in the latter that led to her being selected by Screen International magazine as a Star of Tomorrow in 2008.
Her other stage work includes performances in "Big White Fog" at the Almeida Theatre and "Gethsemane" at the National Theatre, which subsequently toured the UK. Mbatha-Raw made her West End debut playing Ophelia opposite Jude Law in a production of "Hamlet." The production transferred to the United States and became a major success, turning into a hit Broadway show in 2009.
Mbatha-Raw's first film, "Larry Crowne," began shooting in Los Angeles. Directed by Tom Hanks, she starred alongside Julia Roberts, traveling between London and Los Angeles for the production.
Gerald McRaney
CARLTON SHAW
5
Gerald McRaney played Carlton Shaw, a CIA liaison and the handler who gives orders to Steven and Samantha, in the NBC spy drama series "Undercovers." To date, Gerald McRaney has worked on television for over 16 years and has delivered notable performances in numerous series such as "Simon & Simon," "Major Dad," "The Promised Land," "Deadwood," "Jericho," and "JAG." His career has reached new heights, and he is thoroughly enjoying it.
6

He later appeared in the independent film "Get Low," alongside Oscar-nominated actor Robert Duvall, Golden Globe-nominated actor Bill Murray, Oscar winner Sissy Spacek, and Lucas Black. He also co-starred with Liam Neeson and Bradley Cooper in the action-adventure film "The A-Team."
His first television role was a guest appearance on "Night Gallery," followed by several appearances on "Gunsmoke." He then began to appear in numerous television movies, such as "Where the Ladies Go," "The White Shadow," "The Law," and "Roots: The Next Generations." He also appeared in classic series like "The Incredible Hulk," "The Rockford Files," and "How the West Was Won."
In addition, McRaney has appeared in many highly-rated television series. These include the television movies "The John Denver Story," "A Stranger Beside Me," "Not My Son," "The Death of a Centerfold: The Dorothy Stratten Story," "Dream of Murder," and "Someone She Knows." The talented McRaney also crossed over into directing multiple film and television projects, such as "The Two Simons" and "Major Dad," while also serving as a producer on several works. MacIntyre previously played the rogue hero JD Bruce in the series "American Heiress." He has also guest-starred in numerous series including "Nip/Tuck," "It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia," "The Mentalist," "Trauma," and "Bones."

MacIntyre is from Atlanta, Georgia, and graduated from Wake Forest University in North Carolina. He enjoys playing tennis and golf, reading, and traveling. He is single and currently resides in Los Angeles.
Highlights
texts.4:
The first regular series officially picked up for the 2010-2011 season by the five major networks has finally been announced -- Undercovers. This likely comes as no surprise, as the spy comedy created by J.J. Abrams and Josh Reims (Brothers & Sisters) has been one of NBC's hottest new series for 2013. NBC's President of Primetime Entertainment, Angela Bromstad, lavished praise on J.J. Abrams when announcing the pickup, stating that J.J.'s involvement was "something worth celebrating in a big way."
Synopsis
Overview
Stills
9
Undercovers was created by the renowned writer, producer, and director J.J. Abrams, known for series such as Lost, Alias, and Fringe, along with producer and writer Josh Reims from Brothers & Sisters and What About Brian. It is a spy drama filled with sexiness, humor, and action, exploring the idea that in the world of espionage, working as a married couple has its pros and cons, but danger is a constant. On the surface, Steven Bloom (played by Boris Kodjoe
) and his wife Samantha (played by Gugu Mbatha-Raw) are a happy couple. They own a small catering company in Los Angeles and lead a typical middle-class life. Samantha's sister, Lizzy (played by
Jessica Parker Kennedy
), also helps out at the company, but she is not particularly ambitious.
In reality, Steven and Samantha are top agents trained by the
Central Intelligence Agency
(CIA). They fell in love five years ago while on a mission and subsequently decided to retire. When their friend and colleague Leo Nash (played by
Carter MacIntyre
) mysteriously disappears while tracking a Russian arms magnate, CIA official Carlton Shaw (played by Gerald McRaney) is forced to ask the Bloom couple to come out of retirement. The concern is that Nash possesses sensitive intelligence, and its potential leak could have dire consequences. They are tasked with finding and rescuing Nash.
The Blooms are initially reluctant to get involved but ultimately cannot refuse. Furthermore, they quickly discover that being "undercover spies" is more tense, thrilling, exciting, and romantic than being "full-time spies"—elements that had been missing from their marriage for a long time.
First Episode Synopsis
texts.5:
Steven Bloom and Samantha Bloom have been out of the CIA for five years. They are married, have started a family, and together with Samantha's sister Lizzy, they run a small catering business, living a normal life. Their marriage is stable and happy, and everything seems perfect. An international hotel chain is preparing to host a series of events and hires the Blooms as catering consultants. The Blooms never imagined that their peaceful life was about to end...
10
The Blooms' former CIA supervisor, Agent Garlton Shaw, locates them through the hotel and asks them to return to work for the Agency. The Blooms flatly refuse: "We don't want to lose the life we have now. We've worked hard for five years in Los Angeles to build what we have." However, Shaw's visit stirs up old memories for the Blooms... Days later, they embark on a new mission. Samantha's former field partner, Leo Nash, has mysteriously disappeared while tracking Russian arms dealer Alexander Schlotsky, and the CIA suspects Leo may have turned. Leo is one of the CIA's top operatives, known for his elusive nature. The Blooms have a close history with him; perhaps only they know where to find him—which is the main reason the CIA has recalled them.
The Blooms quickly discover that Leo was last seen in
Madrid
, Spain, and rush there to investigate with the help of the local CIA action officer, Bill Hoyt (played by Ben Schwartz). Bill makes no secret of his admiration for Steven, and his flattery makes Samantha uncomfortable. Steven, for his part, is also uneasy about Samantha and Leo's "complicated past."
They sneak into a bank to review security footage, pose as wedding guests to find Leo's contact... After this series of by-the-book "spycraft," they finally uncover the mystery behind Leo's disappearance. The Blooms' blood starts pumping... It's been a long time since they felt this kind of excitement. Perhaps it's only in "the game" that they can rediscover their old passion.
The mission may be over, but the Blooms' life as spies is far from finished. It's just that... now they are catering contractors by day and operatives by night.
Synopsis of Episode 3
Episode 3 Stills
11
texts.6:
In Episode 3 of Undercovers, an individual claims to possess crucial information regarding a code-breaking device that could potentially expose the true identities of every CIA agent. Shaw orders Steven and Samantha Bloom to travel to Berlin to verify the intelligence. They quickly discover that the informant has been killed. With the assistance of Bill Hoyt and Leo Nash, they uncover the truth behind the entire incident. Meanwhile, Steven and Samantha continue to struggle with the awkward dynamic of being both partners and spouses while on missions.
12
Brief Review
Despite the production team's repeated denials of any resemblance to Alias, the two shows do share factual similarities (such as the chase sequence in the opening minutes). This is not necessarily a bad thing—spy shows often rely on familiar tropes, and if a series cannot achieve the "revolutionary innovation" of a show like Chuck, it might be better to stick to convention.
13
Some expressed concern that the show, featuring an all-Black lead cast (a first in recent years), might not be accepted by audiences. This worry seems somewhat justified, but not entirely—both lead actors are "quite attractive" Black individuals, though they have limited acting experience and are less familiar to viewers. "Spotlighting newcomers" has been J.J. Abrams' consistent approach, and the "newcomers" he selects are generally reliable (e.g., Keri Russell, Evangeline Lilly, Jennifer Garner, Anna Torv).
This series feels more like a marital relationship drama or a light comedy than a traditional spy thriller. It is the most relaxed, straightforward, and least intellectually demanding of all J.J. Abrams' works—even simpler than the relationship drama Felicity. Furthermore, Steven and Samantha's adversaries are all paper tigers, even more inept than the enemies faced by Christopher Chance in Human Target. At least in the premiere episode, the Blooms never encounter any real danger.
Some have bluntly pointed out that if this series were not associated with J.J. Abrams in any way, it would not have garnered its current level of attention.
Series Cancellation
texts.7:
After another painful decline in ratings, NBC officially announced the cancellation of J.J. Abrams' series Undercovers (5.8 million viewers, 1.3 rating in the 18-49 demographic). NBC will air the three remaining completed episodes (episodes 8-10) as scheduled. As for whether episodes 11-13 might ever air, that's anyone's guess. This is the second series bearing J.J. Abrams' name to be canceled mid-season, the previous one being Six Degrees. Undercovers had also received a four-episode back-order. Similarly, Undercovers' ratings were struggling on the edge, but the show's creativity was certainly commendable and deserved more attention.

She subsequently performed in Antony and Cleopatra at the Royal Exchange Theatre in Manchester and as the lead, Juliet, in Romeo and Juliet, earning her a nomination for the Manchester Evening News Best Actress Award in 2005.
Her British television credits include Spooks, Doctor Who, Marple: A Murder Is Announced, Bonekickers, and Foyle's War. It was her role in the latter that led to her being selected by Screen International magazine as a Star of Tomorrow in 2008.
Her other stage work includes performances in "Big White Fog" at the Almeida Theatre and "Gethsemane" at the National Theatre, which subsequently toured the UK. Mbatha-Raw made her West End debut playing Ophelia opposite Jude Law in a production of "Hamlet." The production transferred to the United States and became a major success, turning into a hit Broadway show in 2009.
Mbatha-Raw's first film, "Larry Crowne," began shooting in Los Angeles. Directed by Tom Hanks, she starred alongside Julia Roberts, traveling between London and Los Angeles for the production.
Gerald McRaney
CARLTON SHAW
5
Gerald McRaney played Carlton Shaw, a CIA liaison and the handler who gives orders to Steven and Samantha, in the NBC spy drama series "Undercovers." To date, Gerald McRaney has worked on television for over 16 years and has delivered notable performances in numerous series such as "Simon & Simon," "Major Dad," "The Promised Land," "Deadwood," "Jericho," and "JAG." His career has reached new heights, and he is thoroughly enjoying it.
6

In the previous season, he also made his Broadway debut in Horton Foote's play "Dividing the Estate." He later appeared in the independent film "Get Low," alongside Oscar-nominated actor Robert Duvall, Golden Globe-nominated actor Bill Murray, Oscar winner Sissy Spacek, and Lucas Black. He also co-starred with Liam Neeson and Bradley Cooper in the action-adventure film "The A-Team."
His first television role was a guest appearance on "Night Gallery," followed by several appearances on "Gunsmoke." He then began to appear in numerous television movies, such as "Where the Ladies Go," "The White Shadow," "The Law," and "Roots: The Next Generations." He also appeared in classic series like "The Incredible Hulk," "The Rockford Files," and "How the West Was Won."
In addition, McRaney has appeared in many highly-rated television series. These include the television movies "The John Denver Story," "A Stranger Beside Me," "Not My Son," "The Death of a Centerfold: The Dorothy Stratten Story," "Dream of Murder," and "Someone She Knows." The talented McRaney also crossed over into directing multiple film and television projects, such as "The Two Simons" and "Major Dad," while also serving as a producer on several works. He has collaborated with his wife, actress Delta Burke.
Carter MacIntyre
LEO NASH
7
Carter MacIntyre portrayed LEO NASH in the NBC spy drama series "Undercovers," an elusive agent working under Steven and Samantha (played by Boris Kodjoe and Gugu Mbatha-Raw). MacIntyre previously played the rogue hero JD Bruce in the series "American Heiress." He has also guest-starred in numerous series including "Nip/Tuck," "It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia," "The Mentalist," "Trauma," and "Bones."
8
He has also appeared in several films, including "The Choice of Fate," starring Louis Gossett Jr. and Lauren Holly, and "The Truth," starring John Heard.
MacIntyre is from Atlanta, Georgia, and graduated from Wake Forest University in North Carolina. He enjoys playing tennis and golf, reading, and traveling. He is single and currently resides in Los Angeles.
Highlights

The first regular series officially picked up for the 2010-2011 season by the five major networks has finally been announced -- Undercovers. This likely comes as no surprise, as the spy comedy created by J.J. Abrams and Josh Reims (Brothers & Sisters) has been one of NBC's hottest new series for 2013. NBC's President of Primetime Entertainment, Angela Bromstad, lavished praise on J.J. Abrams when announcing the pickup, stating that J.J.'s involvement was "something worth celebrating in a big way."
Synopsis
Overview
Stills
9
Undercovers was created by the renowned writer, producer, and director J.J. Abrams, known for series such as Lost, Alias, and Fringe, along with producer and writer Josh Reims from Brothers & Sisters and What About Brian. It is a spy drama filled with sexiness, humor, and action, exploring the idea that in the world of espionage, working as a married couple has its pros and cons, but danger is a constant. On the surface, Steven Bloom (played by Boris Kodjoe
) and his wife Samantha (played by Gugu Mbatha-Raw) are a happy couple. They own a small catering company in Los Angeles and lead a typical middle-class life. Samantha's sister, Lizzy (played by
Jessica Parker Kennedy
), also helps out at the company, but she is not particularly ambitious.
In reality, Steven and Samantha are top agents trained by the
Central Intelligence Agency
(CIA). They fell in love five years ago while on a mission and subsequently decided to retire. When their friend and colleague Leo Nash (played by
Carter MacIntyre
) mysteriously disappears while tracking a Russian arms magnate, CIA official Carlton Shaw (played by Gerald McRaney) is forced to ask the Bloom couple to come out of retirement. The concern is that Nash possesses sensitive intelligence, and its potential leak could have dire consequences. They are tasked with finding and rescuing Nash.
The Blooms are initially reluctant to get involved but ultimately cannot refuse. Furthermore, they quickly discover that being "undercover spies" is more tense, thrilling, exciting, and romantic than being "full-time spies"—elements that had been missing from their marriage for a long time.
First Episode Synopsis

Steven Bloom and Samantha Bloom have been out of the CIA for five years. They are married, have started a family, and together with Samantha's sister Lizzy, they run a small catering business, living a normal life. Their marriage is stable and happy, and everything seems perfect. An international hotel chain is preparing to host a series of events and hires the Blooms as catering consultants. The Blooms never imagined that their peaceful life was about to end...
10
The Blooms' former CIA supervisor, Agent Garlton Shaw, locates them through the hotel and asks them to return to work for the Agency. The Blooms flatly refuse: "We don't want to lose the life we have now. We've worked hard for five years in Los Angeles to build what we have." However, Shaw's visit stirs up old memories for the Blooms... Days later, they embark on a new mission. Samantha's former field partner, Leo Nash, has mysteriously disappeared while tracking Russian arms dealer Alexander Schlotsky, and the CIA suspects Leo may have turned. Leo is one of the CIA's top operatives, known for his elusive nature. The Blooms have a close history with him; perhaps only they know where to find him—which is the main reason the CIA has recalled them.
The Blooms quickly discover that Leo was last seen in
Madrid
, Spain, and rush there to investigate with the help of the local CIA action officer, Bill Hoyt (played by Ben Schwartz). Bill makes no secret of his admiration for Steven, and his flattery makes Samantha uncomfortable. Steven, for his part, is also uneasy about Samantha and Leo's "complicated past."
They sneak into a bank to review security footage, pose as wedding guests to find Leo's contact... After this series of by-the-book "spycraft," they finally uncover the mystery behind Leo's disappearance. The Blooms' blood starts pumping... It's been a long time since they felt this kind of excitement. Perhaps it's only in "the game" that they can rediscover their old passion.
The mission may be over, but the Blooms' life as spies is far from finished. It's just that... now they are catering contractors by day and operatives by night.
Synopsis of Episode 3
Episode 3 Stills
11

In Episode 3 of Undercovers, an individual claims to possess crucial information regarding a code-breaking device that could potentially expose the true identities of every CIA agent. Shaw orders Steven and Samantha Bloom to travel to Berlin to verify the intelligence. They quickly discover that the informant has been killed. With the assistance of Bill Hoyt and Leo Nash, they uncover the truth behind the entire incident. Meanwhile, Steven and Samantha continue to struggle with the awkward dynamic of being both partners and spouses while on missions.
12
Brief Review
Despite the production team's repeated denials of any resemblance to Alias, the two shows do share factual similarities (such as the chase sequence in the opening minutes). This is not necessarily a bad thing—spy shows often rely on familiar tropes, and if a series cannot achieve the "revolutionary innovation" of a show like Chuck, it might be better to stick to convention.
13
Some expressed concern that the show, featuring an all-Black lead cast (a first in recent years), might not be accepted by audiences. This worry seems somewhat justified, but not entirely—both lead actors are "quite attractive" Black individuals, though they have limited acting experience and are less familiar to viewers. "Spotlighting newcomers" has been J.J. Abrams' consistent approach, and the "newcomers" he selects are generally reliable (e.g., Keri Russell, Evangeline Lilly, Jennifer Garner, Anna Torv).
This series feels more like a marital relationship drama or a light comedy than a traditional spy thriller. It is the most relaxed, straightforward, and least intellectually demanding of all J.J. Abrams' works—even simpler than the relationship drama Felicity. Furthermore, Steven and Samantha's adversaries are all paper tigers, even more inept than the enemies faced by Christopher Chance in Human Target. At least in the premiere episode, the Blooms never encounter any real danger.
Some have bluntly pointed out that if this series were not associated with J.J. Abrams in any way, it would not have garnered its current level of attention.
Series Cancellation

After another painful decline in ratings, NBC officially announced the cancellation of J.J. Abrams' series Undercovers (5.8 million viewers, 1.3 rating in the 18-49 demographic). NBC will air the three remaining completed episodes (episodes 8-10) as scheduled. As for whether episodes 11-13 might ever air, that's anyone's guess. This is the second series bearing J.J. Abrams' name to be canceled mid-season, the previous one being Six Degrees. Undercovers had also received a four-episode back-order. Similarly, Undercovers' ratings were struggling on the edge, but the show's creativity was certainly commendable and deserved more attention.

The History of ABC’s New York Television Studios

By Bobby Ellerbee and Eyes Of A Generation.com
Preface and Acknowledgement
This is the first part of a unique, historical report on the creation of the broadcast facilities  
and studios used by The American Broadcasting Company. The first part of the story takes  
place in New York, and is covered here. The second part of the ABC studios story lays out  
the history of ABC’s growth on the West Coast and is about the Los Angeles studios.
As ABC’s official historical archives are actually quite scarce, it took an extra deep dive to come  
up with some of the ultra rare texts, photos, personal recollections and memoirs that are included  
in this report. For much of the network’s history, photos in the studios, except for a few rare  
publicity shots, were not permitted by anyone, so there will not be as many as in my NBC and  
CBS reports, but there will be some exceptionally interesting information presented here that  
only a handful of people have ever seen.
As has been the case with my four prior historical reports on NBC New York, NBC West Coast  
and CBS New York, CBS West Coast, this effort would not have been possible without the help  
of many current and former ABC staffers from every area of the network and every era. I would  
like to offer my thanks to those dozens and dozens that helped, but especially to John Fider, Dick  
Roes, Donald Launer, Bob Franklin, Bill Freiberger, Howie Zeidman and Bill Rigo.
This story is told to the best of our abilities, as a great deal of the information on these facilities  
is now gone…like so many of the men and women who worked there. I’ve told this as concisely  
as possible, but some elements are dependent on the memories of those who were there many  
years ago, and from conclusions drawn from research. If you can add to this with facts or photos,  
please contact me, as this is an ongoing project.
This presentation is presented as a public service by the world’s ultimate destination for  
television’s living history…Eyes of a Generation.com –Bobby Ellerbee

In The Beginning, There Was WJZ Radio…
As mentioned in the preface above, there is not very much in the way of historical archives from  
ABC. Possibly because of this, there is, and always has been an informal internal narrative of the  
history of the network among many of the network’s employees. We are quite fortunate to have  
located and spoken with some of these key people and have their assistance in telling this story.  
There is no better way to tell this story than by using their photos, recollections and memoirs and  
that kicks in just a few pages down.
Allow me to set the stage with a history that, believe it or not, it starts with David Sarnoff.
By 1919, 28 year old Sarnoff was the commercial manager of American Marconi in New York.  
That same year, British Marconi made an offer to General Electric to buy the worldwide rights to  
the Alexanderson Alternator technology, which was vital for transatlantic communication. The  
prospect of a foreign company controlling international communications set off alarm bells in  
Washington, and the government approached GE with a counter offer. If GE would place the  
Alternator technology in a new subsidiary company, they would be allowed to operate the  
international wireless circuits for both government and commercial traffic. To sweeten the deal,  
the Navy agreed to turn over all the wireless patents it received through its wartime research.
The new GE subsidiary company was named the Radio Corporation of America. At the  
helm was Owen Young as Chairman, Ernst Alexanderson as Chief Engineer and David Sarnoff  
as General Manager. Within months, AT&T, Westinghouse and a big consumer of international  
wireless services, United Fruit Company, bought up all the RCA shares.

## [PDF page 3]
By 1921, commercial broadcasting stations begun to appear with 28 springing up that year,  
including the Westinghouse-owned 50,000 watt WJZ in New Jersey. With the July 2, 1921  
World Heavyweight Championship fight between America's Jack Dempsey and France's George  
Carpentier looming, everyone in New York was anxious for a speedy way to know the details  
and outcome. David Sarnoff decided RCA should arrange to broadcast the fight on WJZ. It was a  
radio first; a publicity coup for RCA and Westinghouse, and it sold lots of radios!
With Westinghouse in a good mood, Sarnoff convinced them to allow RCA to take over WJZ.  
With the buyout, RCA moved the license from Newark to New York City and the transmitter nd  
and studios to the Aeolian Building on West 42  Street.  This was RCA’s first broadcast  
property.
In the summer of 1924, AT&T's management began to consider getting out of the broadcast  
business, and in July 1926, AT&T agreed to sell their New York City station, WEAF, to RCA.
When RCA acquired WEAF, their studio and office was in the AT&T Building at 195  
Broadway. Less than a year after RCA created NBC, the company’s first made-to-order studios  
were ready, and on October 1, 1927, NBC moved into the new facilities on the twelfth and  
thirteenth floors of 711 5th Avenue, with WEAF and WJZ now at the same location.

**ABC Records** was an American record label founded in New York City in 1955. It originated as the main popular music label operated by the Am-Par Record Corporation. Am-Par also created the Impulse! jazz label in 1960. It acquired many labels before ABC was sold to MCA Records in 1979. ABC produced music in a variety of genres: pop, rock, jazz, country, rhythm and blues, soundtrack, gospel, and polka. In addition to producing records, ABC licensed masters from independent record producers, and purchased regionally released records for national distribution.
The label was initially called **Am-Par Records** (1955), but quickly changed to **ABC-Paramount Records** (1955–1966), and then renamed **ABC Records** in 1966.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-:1-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-:0-2)

In the 1940s and early 1950s, the Federal Communications Commission took action against the Anti-competitive practices of movie studios and broadcasting companies, forcing the Radio Corporation of America (RCA) to sell the Blue Network, the sister network of NBC Red Network, in 1943. The Blue Network was purchased by Edward J. Noble, who changed the company's name to the American Broadcasting Company (ABC) in 1946. In 1953, ABC merged with United Paramount Theatres, the divested former exhibition/cinema division of Paramount Pictures, with the newly-merged corporation, American Broadcasting-Paramount Theatres (AB-PT) chaired by former Paramount Theaters executive Leonard Goldenson and headquartered at 1501 Broadway in New York City, above the Paramount Theater in Times Square.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-Kahn-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-4)

### ABC-Paramount Records
[edit]
ABC Paramount 78rpm record and original sleeve
American Broadcasting-Paramount Theatres formed a records division, incorporating the Am-Par Record Corporation on June 14, 1955 with Samuel H. Clark as its first president.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-nysc-6) By August 1955, the unit was organized with AMPCO (ASCAP) and PAMCO ([BMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadcast_Music,_Inc. "Broadcast Music, Inc.")) as subsidiary publishing units.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7) Though the record label was established as Am-Par, no records were released until after the division's name was changed to ABC-Paramount in September 1955.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-:1-1)
Eydie Gorme was the company's first signed artist. The company recorded its first single record, "Sincerely Yours" and "Come Home", both by Gorme. Alec Templeton's "Smart Alec" was the company's first LP recorded, also in September 1955.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)
One of Gorme's singles was its first release in January 1956.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-8) "Chain Gang" by Bobby Scott in February 1956 was the company's first national hit. George Hamilton IV's "A Rose and a Baby Ruth" single was Am-Paramount's first million-selling single in October 1956.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)

### ABC-Paramount Records
In 1957, the company had two million-selling singles: in June with "Diana" by Paul Anka and in October with "At the Hop" by Danny & the Juniors. Am-Paramount Records in May 1958 debuted the Apt subsidiary label with its first million-selling single, "Little Star" by the Elegants, released the same month.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)
Chancellor Records had Am-Par Record Corporation handle its distribution starting in 1957 and started a trend.
Am-Par purchased Grand Award Records including the newly formed Command Records label, in 1959.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7) The company started a second label for jazz, Impulse! Records, in November 1960.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-9) Impulse released its first four records in January 1961.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)
The company had artists that earned three Grammy Awards in 1960.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7) While in January 1961, the company purchased Westminster Records, a classical label. Thus Am-Par Record had a label for each music genre.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)

### ABC-Paramount Records
Am-Par Record Corporation was renamed to ABC-Paramount Records, Inc. on December 7, 1961.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-nysc-6) The company opened a Los Angeles office in January 1962. Ray Charles formed Tangerine Records in March 1962 and arranged for ABC-Paramount to distribute Tangerine's records. The company formed Jet Record Distributors based in Long Island City, N.Y. as its local distributor. Also in 1962, the company had acquired Music Guild label and library for Westminster Records.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)
In 1965, Clark was promoted to vice-president in charge of AB-PT's non-broadcast operations. National sales manager Larry Newton was named ABC-Paramount president.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb-5) On January 4, 1965, vice-president in charge of sales Larry Newton was promoted to president of ABC-Paramount Records. The previous president, Sam Clark was promoted to director of theater operations for American Broadcasting-Paramount Theatres. Newton's first action as president was to restart Apt Records as a teen-oriented West Coast base label under Irwin Garr.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-10)
**Apt Records** was a sub-label from ABC-Paramount Records. The label was started in 1958 and released only singles until it was shelved in 1966. ABC briefly reactivated Apt twice, in 1969 and 1972, and also used the Apt name on a line of budget-priced 8-track and cassette tapes in 1970.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-11) The name was derived from ABC-Paramount's parent company, American Broadcasting-Paramount Theatres.
Label variants included:

### ABC-Paramount Records
*   1958-1966: Black label with multi-color logo at top  
*   1965: Black and white label with new logo at left (in conjunction with the above label)  
*   1969-1972: Yellow label with orange APT logo and "abc RECORDS" logo at top
In June 1966, the label was renamed ABC Records,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-:0-2) and the company acquired New Deal Record Service Corp., a rack-jobbing and record distribution company, along with its affiliates.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-12)
In 1967, Dunhill Records was purchased from Lou Adler.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-13) In 1970, ABC and Dunhill moved its headquarters to Los Angeles. Newton was promoted to vice-president in charge of ABC Pictures. Dunhill co-owner Jay Lasker was named president and referred to the combined operations as ABC/Dunhill. At that time ABC had another five labels: Westminster, Command, Probe, Impulse!, and Bluesway.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb0-14)
At the August 29, 1970 Directors Guild meeting, ABC/Dunhill launched a number of marketing initiatives. The company planned to have writers create a broader music for the catalog market. Imprints Probe and Apt were relaunched, Probe as a label which held the international rights to ABC's albums and Apt as a label which released budget cassettes and 8-track tapes. Jazz dropped from Impulse!'s cover for a new slogan: "University Series of Fine Recordings" and two new series were launched: Audio Treasury and Westminster Gold for classic and youth fare, respectively.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-15)

**ABC Records** was an American record label founded in New York City in 1955. It originated as the main popular music label operated by the Am-Par Record Corporation. Am-Par also created the Impulse! jazz label in 1960. It acquired many labels before ABC was sold to MCA Records in 1979. ABC produced music in a variety of genres: pop, rock, jazz, country, rhythm and blues, soundtrack, gospel, and polka. In addition to producing records, ABC licensed masters from independent record producers, and purchased regionally released records for national distribution.
The label was initially called **Am-Par Records** (1955), but quickly changed to **ABC-Paramount Records** (1955–1966), and then renamed **ABC Records** in 1966.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-:1-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-:0-2)

## [PDF page 1]
1
The History of ABC’s New York Television Studios
Part 1 of 2  
By Bobby Ellerbee and Eyes Of A Generation.com
Preface and Acknowledgement
This is the first part of a unique, historical report on the creation of the broadcast facilities  
and studios used by The American Broadcasting Company. The first part of the story takes  
place in New York, and is covered here. The second part of the ABC studios story lays out  
the history of ABC’s growth on the West Coast and is about the Los Angeles studios.
As ABC’s official historical archives are actually quite scarce, it took an extra deep dive to come  
up with some of the ultra rare texts, photos, personal recollections and memoirs that are included  
in this report. For much of the network’s history, photos in the studios, except for a few rare  
publicity shots, were not permitted by anyone, so there will not be as many as in my NBC and  
CBS reports, but there will be some exceptionally interesting information presented here that  
only a handful of people have ever seen.
As has been the case with my four prior historical reports on NBC New York, NBC West Coast  
and CBS New York, CBS West Coast, this effort would not have been possible without the help  
of many current and former ABC staffers from every area of the network and every era. I would  
like to offer my thanks to those dozens and dozens that helped, but especially to John Fider, Dick  
Roes, Donald Launer, Bob Franklin, Bill Freiberger, Howie Zeidman and Bill Rigo.
This story is told to the best of our abilities, as a great deal of the information on these facilities  
is now gone…like so many of the men and women who worked there. I’ve told this as concisely  
as possible, but some elements are dependent on the memories of those who were there many  
years ago, and from conclusions drawn from research. If you can add to this with facts or photos,  
please contact me, as this is an ongoing project.
This presentation is presented as a public service by the world’s ultimate destination for  
television’s living history…Eyes of a Generation.com –Bobby Ellerbee

## [PDF page 3]
3
In The Beginning, There Was WJZ Radio…
As mentioned in the preface above, there is not very much in the way of historical archives from  
ABC. Possibly because of this, there is, and always has been an informal internal narrative of the  
history of the network among many of the network’s employees. We are quite fortunate to have  
located and spoken with some of these key people and have their assistance in telling this story.  
There is no better way to tell this story than by using their photos, recollections and memoirs and  
that kicks in just a few pages down.
Allow me to set the stage with a history that, believe it or not, it starts with David Sarnoff.
By 1919, 28 year old Sarnoff was the commercial manager of American Marconi in New York.  
That same year, British Marconi made an offer to General Electric to buy the worldwide rights to  
the Alexanderson Alternator technology, which was vital for transatlantic communication. The  
prospect of a foreign company controlling international communications set off alarm bells in  
Washington, and the government approached GE with a counter offer. If GE would place the  
Alternator technology in a new subsidiary company, they would be allowed to operate the  
international wireless circuits for both government and commercial traffic. To sweeten the deal,  
the Navy agreed to turn over all the wireless patents it received through its wartime research.
The new GE subsidiary company was named the Radio Corporation of America. At the  
helm was Owen Young as Chairman, Ernst Alexanderson as Chief Engineer and David Sarnoff  
as General Manager. Within months, AT&T, Westinghouse and a big consumer of international  
wireless services, United Fruit Company, bought up all the RCA shares.
texts.5:
## [PDF page 3]
By 1921, commercial broadcasting stations begun to appear with 28 springing up that year,  
including the Westinghouse-owned 50,000 watt WJZ in New Jersey. With the July 2, 1921  
World Heavyweight Championship fight between America's Jack Dempsey and France's George  
Carpentier looming, everyone in New York was anxious for a speedy way to know the details  
and outcome. David Sarnoff decided RCA should arrange to broadcast the fight on WJZ. It was a  
radio first; a publicity coup for RCA and Westinghouse, and it sold lots of radios!

**ABC Records** was an American record label founded in New York City in 1955. It originated as the main popular music label operated by the Am-Par Record Corporation. Am-Par also created the Impulse! jazz label in 1960. It acquired many labels before ABC was sold to MCA Records in 1979. ABC produced music in a variety of genres: pop, rock, jazz, country, rhythm and blues, soundtrack, gospel, and polka. In addition to producing records, ABC licensed masters from independent record producers, and purchased regionally released records for national distribution.
The label was initially called **Am-Par Records** (1955), but quickly changed to **ABC-Paramount Records** (1955–1966), and then renamed **ABC Records** in 1966.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-:1-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-:0-2)

In the 1940s and early 1950s, the Federal Communications Commission took action against the Anti-competitive practices of movie studios and broadcasting companies, forcing the Radio Corporation of America (RCA) to sell the Blue Network, the sister network of NBC Red Network, in 1943. The Blue Network was purchased by Edward J. Noble, who changed the company's name to the American Broadcasting Company (ABC) in 1946. In 1953, ABC merged with United Paramount Theatres, the divested former exhibition/cinema division of Paramount Pictures, with the newly-merged corporation, American Broadcasting-Paramount Theatres (AB-PT) chaired by former Paramount Theaters executive Leonard Goldenson and headquartered at 1501 Broadway in New York City, above the Paramount Theater in Times Square.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-Kahn-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-4)

### ABC-Paramount Records
[edit]
ABC Paramount 78rpm record and original sleeve
American Broadcasting-Paramount Theatres formed a records division, incorporating the Am-Par Record Corporation on June 14, 1955 with Samuel H. Clark as its first president.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-nysc-6) By August 1955, the unit was organized with AMPCO (ASCAP) and PAMCO ([BMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadcast_Music,_Inc. "Broadcast Music, Inc.")) as subsidiary publishing units.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7) Though the record label was established as Am-Par, no records were released until after the division's name was changed to ABC-Paramount in September 1955.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-:1-1)
Eydie Gorme was the company's first signed artist. The company recorded its first single record, "Sincerely Yours" and "Come Home", both by Gorme. Alec Templeton's "Smart Alec" was the company's first LP recorded, also in September 1955.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)
One of Gorme's singles was its first release in January 1956.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-8) "Chain Gang" by Bobby Scott in February 1956 was the company's first national hit. George Hamilton IV's "A Rose and a Baby Ruth" single was Am-Paramount's first million-selling single in October 1956.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)

### ABC-Paramount Records
In 1957, the company had two million-selling singles: in June with "Diana" by Paul Anka and in October with "At the Hop" by Danny & the Juniors. Am-Paramount Records in May 1958 debuted the Apt subsidiary label with its first million-selling single, "Little Star" by the Elegants, released the same month.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)
Chancellor Records had Am-Par Record Corporation handle its distribution starting in 1957 and started a trend.
Am-Par purchased Grand Award Records including the newly formed Command Records label, in 1959.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7) The company started a second label for jazz, Impulse! Records, in November 1960.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-9) Impulse released its first four records in January 1961.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)
The company had artists that earned three Grammy Awards in 1960.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7) While in January 1961, the company purchased Westminster Records, a classical label. Thus Am-Par Record had a label for each music genre.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)

### ABC-Paramount Records
Am-Par Record Corporation was renamed to ABC-Paramount Records, Inc. on December 7, 1961.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-nysc-6) The company opened a Los Angeles office in January 1962. Ray Charles formed Tangerine Records in March 1962 and arranged for ABC-Paramount to distribute Tangerine's records. The company formed Jet Record Distributors based in Long Island City, N.Y. as its local distributor. Also in 1962, the company had acquired Music Guild label and library for Westminster Records.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)

The previous president, Sam Clark was promoted to director of theater operations for American Broadcasting-Paramount Theatres. Newton's first action as president was to restart Apt Records as a teen-oriented West Coast base label under Irwin Garr.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-10)
**Apt Records** was a sub-label from ABC-Paramount Records. The label was started in 1958 and released only singles until it was shelved in 1966. ABC briefly reactivated Apt twice, in 1969 and 1972, and also used the Apt name on a line of budget-priced 8-track and cassette tapes in 1970.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-11) The name was derived from ABC-Paramount's parent company, American Broadcasting-Paramount Theatres.
Label variants included:

### ABC-Paramount Records
*   1958-1966: Black label with multi-color logo at top  
*   1965: Black and white label with new logo at left (in conjunction with the above label)  
*   1969-1972: Yellow label with orange APT logo and "abc RECORDS" logo at top
In June 1966, the label was renamed ABC Records,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-:0-2) and the company acquired New Deal Record Service Corp., a rack-jobbing and record distribution company, along with its affiliates.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-12)
In 1967, Dunhill Records was purchased from Lou Adler.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-13) In 1970, ABC and Dunhill moved its headquarters to Los Angeles. Newton was promoted to vice-president in charge of ABC Pictures. Dunhill co-owner Jay Lasker was named president and referred to the combined operations as ABC/Dunhill. At that time ABC had another five labels: Westminster, Command, Probe, Impulse!, and Bluesway.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb0-14)
At the August 29, 1970 Directors Guild meeting, ABC/Dunhill launched a number of marketing initiatives. The company planned to have writers create a broader music for the catalog market. Imprints Probe and Apt were relaunched, Probe as a label which held the international rights to ABC's albums and Apt as a label which released budget cassettes and 8-track tapes. Jazz dropped from Impulse!'s cover for a new slogan: "University Series of Fine Recordings" and two new series were launched: Audio Treasury and Westminster Gold for classic and youth fare, respectively.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-15)

Preface and Acknowledgement
This is the first part of a unique, historical report on the creation of the broadcast facilities  
and studios used by The American Broadcasting Company. The first part of the story takes  
place in New York, and is covered here. The second part of the ABC studios story lays out  
the history of ABC’s growth on the West Coast and is about the Los Angeles studios.
As ABC’s official historical archives are actually quite scarce, it took an extra deep dive to come  
up with some of the ultra rare texts, photos, personal recollections and memoirs that are included  
in this report. For much of the network’s history, photos in the studios, except for a few rare  
publicity shots, were not permitted by anyone, so there will not be as many as in my NBC and  
CBS reports, but there will be some exceptionally interesting information presented here that  
only a handful of people have ever seen.
As has been the case with my four prior historical reports on NBC New York, NBC West Coast  
and CBS New York, CBS West Coast, this effort would not have been possible without the help  
of many current and former ABC staffers from every area of the network and every era. I would  
like to offer my thanks to those dozens and dozens that helped, but especially to John Fider, Dick  
Roes, Donald Launer, Bob Franklin, Bill Freiberger, Howie Zeidman and Bill Rigo.

As mentioned in the preface above, there is not very much in the way of historical archives from

history of the network among many of the network’s employees. We are quite fortunate to have  
located and spoken with some of these key people and have their assistance in telling this story.

that kicks in just a few pages down.
Allow me to set the stage with a history that, believe it or not, it starts with David Sarnoff.
By 1919, 28 year old Sarnoff was the commercial manager of American Marconi in New York.  
That same year, British Marconi made an offer to General Electric to buy the worldwide rights to  
the Alexanderson Alternator technology, which was vital for transatlantic communication. The  
prospect of a foreign company controlling international communications set off alarm bells in  
Washington, and the government approached GE with a counter offer. If GE would place the  
Alternator technology in a new subsidiary company, they would be allowed to operate the  
international wireless circuits for both government and commercial traffic. To sweeten the deal,  
the Navy agreed to turn over all the wireless patents it received through its wartime research.
The new GE subsidiary company was named the Radio Corporation of America. At the  
helm was Owen Young as Chairman, Ernst Alexanderson as Chief Engineer and David Sarnoff  
as General Manager. Within months, AT&T, Westinghouse and a big consumer of international  
wireless services, United Fruit Company, bought up all the RCA shares.

## [PDF page 3]
By 1921, commercial broadcasting stations begun to appear with 28 springing up that year,  
including the Westinghouse-owned 50,000 watt WJZ in New Jersey. With the July 2, 1921  
World Heavyweight Championship fight between America's Jack Dempsey and France's George  
Carpentier looming, everyone in New York was anxious for a speedy way to know the details  
and outcome. David Sarnoff decided RCA should arrange to broadcast the fight on WJZ. It was a  
radio first; a publicity coup for RCA and Westinghouse, and it sold lots of radios!
With Westinghouse in a good mood, Sarnoff convinced them to allow RCA to take over WJZ.

property.

business, and in July 1926, AT&T agreed to sell their New York City station, WEAF, to RCA.

Broadway. Less than a year after RCA created NBC, the company’s first made-to-order studios  
were ready, and on October 1, 1927, NBC moved into the new facilities on the twelfth and  
thirteenth floors of 711 5th Avenue, with WEAF and WJZ now at the same location.

Thus Am-Par Record had a label for each music genre.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)

### ABC-Paramount Records
Am-Par Record Corporation was renamed to ABC-Paramount Records, Inc. on December 7, 1961.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-nysc-6) The company opened a Los Angeles office in January 1962. Ray Charles formed Tangerine Records in March 1962 and arranged for ABC-Paramount to distribute Tangerine's records. The company formed Jet Record Distributors based in Long Island City, N.Y. as its local distributor. Also in 1962, the company had acquired Music Guild label and library for Westminster Records.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)
In 1965, Clark was promoted to vice-president in charge of AB-PT's non-broadcast operations. National sales manager Larry Newton was named ABC-Paramount president.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb-5) On January 4, 1965, vice-president in charge of sales Larry Newton was promoted to president of ABC-Paramount Records. The previous president, Sam Clark was promoted to director of theater operations for American Broadcasting-Paramount Theatres. Newton's first action as president was to restart Apt Records as a teen-oriented West Coast base label under Irwin Garr.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-10)
**Apt Records** was a sub-label from ABC-Paramount Records. The label was started in 1958 and released only singles until it was shelved in 1966. ABC briefly reactivated Apt twice, in 1969 and 1972, and also used the Apt name on a line of budget-priced 8-track and cassette tapes in 1970.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-11) The name was derived from ABC-Paramount's parent company, American Broadcasting-Paramount Theatres.
Label variants included:

### ABC-Paramount Records
*   1958-1966: Black label with multi-color logo at top  
*   1965: Black and white label with new logo at left (in conjunction with the above label)  
*   1969-1972: Yellow label with orange APT logo and "abc RECORDS" logo at top
In June 1966, the label was renamed ABC Records,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-:0-2) and the company acquired New Deal Record Service Corp., a rack-jobbing and record distribution company, along with its affiliates.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-12)
In 1967, Dunhill Records was purchased from Lou Adler.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-13) In 1970, ABC and Dunhill moved its headquarters to Los Angeles. Newton was promoted to vice-president in charge of ABC Pictures. Dunhill co-owner Jay Lasker was named president and referred to the combined operations as ABC/Dunhill. At that time ABC had another five labels: Westminster, Command, Probe, Impulse!, and Bluesway.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb0-14)
At the August 29, 1970 Directors Guild meeting, ABC/Dunhill launched a number of marketing initiatives. The company planned to have writers create a broader music for the catalog market. Imprints Probe and Apt were relaunched, Probe as a label which held the international rights to ABC's albums and Apt as a label which released budget cassettes and 8-track tapes. Jazz dropped from Impulse!'s cover for a new slogan: "University Series of Fine Recordings" and two new series were launched: Audio Treasury and Westminster Gold for classic and youth fare, respectively.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-15)

### ABC-Paramount Records
By May 1972, ABC formed the ABC Leisure Group, which included ABC Records, Anchor Records, and ABC Records and Tape Sales, plus a new retail record-store division.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-16) Lasker left ABC to join Ariola America Records in 1975.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-17) He was succeeded by Jerry Rubinstein, who served as company head until 1977.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-18) In November 1972, ABC bought country music company Cartwheel Records.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-19)
In 1974, ABC switched British distribution from EMI to the EMI-distributed Anchor Records, allowing ABC recordings to be issued on the ABC label in the UK, and Anchor records to be distributed by ABC on the Anchor label in the US.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-20) Also in 1974, ABC acquired Famous Music Records Group including Nashville based Dot Records[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-21) then began releasing ABC country music under the ABC/Dot label until January 1979.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb2-22)
In December 1977, Don Biederman was appointed vice president of legal affairs and administration and Richard Green was appointed vice president of business affairs at ABC Records.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-23)

### ABC-Paramount Records
As a cost-cutting measure, ABC Records discarded many master tapes in the 1970s to save storage space. When these recordings were reissued on compact disc in the 1980s, CD versions were often taken from master copies which had less than optimal sound quality.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-24) The company's last president, Steve Diener, was named to that job in 1977 after serving as head of ABC Records' international division.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-25) Because of financial problems except for its Nashville office, ABC Records was sold on January 31, 1979, to MCA Records with ABC Records being its third label likely under a different name.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb2-22) Instead, MCA discontinued ABC Records on March 5, 1979, and[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-26) albums in the ABC catalog still selling well were reissued on MCA.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-27)
Diener died in April 2019, aged 80.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-28)
ABC Records sub-labeled Apt to release singles. In the early 1960s, it bought Westminster, a classical music label. For jazz it created Impulse!. Led by Creed Taylor and Bob Thiele, Impulse! developed a reputation for innovative releases, including albums by John Coltrane from 1961 until his death in 1967. ABC created Bluesway for blues music. Tangerine was formed by Ray Charles to produce his albums and those he produced.
ABC Records bought Dunhill in the summer of 1967, forming ABC Dunhill Records. It also bought Don Robey's record labels, including Duke, Peacock, Back Beat, and Song Bird on May 23, 1973.

### ABC-Paramount Records
In 1974 ABC bought the Famous Music record labels from Gulf and Western, the parent company of Paramount. This acquisition gave ABC Dot, Blue Thumb, and a distribution deal with Sire, which released the first album from the Ramones.
ABC purchased all labels from Enoch Light in October 1959. It acquired Audition, Command,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-command-29)Colortone, and Waldorf Music Hall.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-grand-30)
In 1979, ABC was acquired by MCA for $30 million.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-Kahn-3) It operated briefly as a separate division. MCA was absorbed by the Universal Music Group, which currently distributes recordings for ABC's current sister company, Disney Music Group, worldwide except for Russia.
This is not the same ABC Records that operates in Australia, which is run by the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, although the Ampar label was distributed in Australia in the 1950s and 1960s, first by W&G Records (1955–60) and then by Festival.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-32) Nor is it the sub-label of Voiceprint.

**ABC Records** was an American record label founded in New York City in 1955. It originated as the main popular music label operated by the Am-Par Record Corporation. Am-Par also created the Impulse! jazz label in 1960. It acquired many labels before ABC was sold to MCA Records in 1979. ABC produced music in a variety of genres: pop, rock, jazz, country, rhythm and blues, soundtrack, gospel, and polka. In addition to producing records, ABC licensed masters from independent record producers, and purchased regionally released records for national distribution.
The label was initially called **Am-Par Records** (1955), but quickly changed to **ABC-Paramount Records** (1955–1966), and then renamed **ABC Records** in 1966.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-:1-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-:0-2)
texts.1: In the 1940s and early 1950s, the Federal Communications Commission took action against the Anti-competitive practices of movie studios and broadcasting companies, forcing the Radio Corporation of America (RCA) to sell the Blue Network, the sister network of NBC Red Network, in 1943. The Blue Network was purchased by Edward J. Noble, who changed the company's name to the American Broadcasting Company (ABC) in 1946. In 1953, ABC merged with United Paramount Theatres, the divested former exhibition/cinema division of Paramount Pictures, with the newly-merged corporation, American Broadcasting-Paramount Theatres (AB-PT) chaired by former Paramount Theaters executive Leonard Goldenson and headquartered at 1501 Broadway in New York City, above the Paramount Theater in Times Square.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-Kahn-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-4)

"Broadcast Music, Inc.")) as subsidiary publishing units.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7) Though the record label was established as Am-Par, no records were released until after the division's name was changed to ABC-Paramount in September 1955.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-:1-1)

Alec Templeton's "Smart Alec" was the company's first LP recorded, also in September 1955.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)

George Hamilton IV's "A Rose and a Baby Ruth" single was Am-Paramount's first million-selling single in October 1956.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Records#cite_note-bb1-7)
